## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. - find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.

Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. - fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

---
title: "1.7 Definition of Done for Non-Software Products"
status: published
slug: "a-csm/section-1-team-development/1.7-definition-of-done-for-non-software-products"
sidebar:

---

The Definition of Done is not just a checklist - it is a reminder and a way of creating a quality culture within the team. When every team member knows what "Done" means, quality becomes a shared responsibility rather than something imposed from outside.

### When Does a Definition of Done Work Well?

A Definition of Done works best when the team is building a consistent type of output on a regular basis. The key is that the nature of the work is similar enough that the same quality standards apply across items.

**Examples where DoD works well for non-software products:**
- **A website content team** producing blog entries meet: accessibility guidelines, branding, have h2 and h3 tags, have an image, ...
- **A marketing team** creating campaign materials that must follow brand guidelines, legal review, and approval workflows
- **A policy team** writing regulatory documents that need consistent formatting, stakeholder review, and compliance checks

In each case, the team produces similar outputs repeatedly, so a shared definition of "Done" helps maintain quality and consistency.

### When Does a Definition of Done Not Work?
A Definition of Done does not work well when the nature of the work changes frequently. If the team's output is different every time, for example, a team that handles a mix of event planning, strategic reports, vendor negotiations, and office moves. There is no consistent set of quality criteria that applies across all those types of work. In these situations, quality standards may need to be defined per item or per type of work rather than as a single team-wide DoD.

### Creating a Non-Software Definition of Done

When building a DoD for a non-software product, focus on:

1. **What quality standards apply consistently** across the things your team produces?
2. **What steps must always happen** before work can be considered complete? (e.g., peer review, stakeholder sign-off, accessibility check)
3. **What would embarrass the team** if it were missed? Those items belong in your DoD.

### Assignment
Think about a non-software product, i.e. restaurant, hotel cleaning, . Draft a Definition of Done for that team's work. Include:

1. What type of output does the team produce on a regular basis?
2. What are the quality standards that should apply to every item?
3. Why would this DoD help create a quality culture on the team?

If the team's work varies too much for a single DoD, explain why and describe what you would do instead.

Write your response in 150-250 words.

Cynefin is hard to wrap your head around. It took me over two years to start to get it. But once you do, it changes how you see problems - and why certain approaches work in some situations and fail in others.

Cynefin (pronounced "kuh-NEV-in") is a sensemaking framework created by Dave Snowden. It helps us recognize that different kinds of problems need fundamentally different approaches. It has four main domains: Clear, Complicated, Complex, and Chaotic.

![](../images/323595-framework-scaled-1024x1024-1-600x600-1.png)

### Clear (formerly Simple/Obvious)

In my CSM classes, I teach Cynefin using examples from everyday life. I start by asking: "How many of you know how to change the batteries in a flashlight?" Most hands go up. "What about the batteries in your car remote?" A few hands drop. "What about changing a tire on your car?" A few more drop.

These are all examples of Clear problems. The relationship between cause and effect is obvious. You sense the problem, categorize it based on what you already know (or can easily learn), and respond using a known best practice. Once you have learned the solution, it stays learned.

### Complicated

Next I ask: "Can you take apart your car engine and put it back together?" Almost nobody can. But a trained mechanic can, because they know the sequence - take it apart step by step, then reassemble in roughly the reverse order.

This is a Complicated problem. It is made up of many Clear steps done in sequence, but you need expertise or analysis to figure out the right sequence. The approach is: sense the problem, analyze it (get expert help, watch videos, create a plan), then respond. The traditional waterfall model works well here because the problem is knowable in advance - you just need to do the analysis first.

### Complex

Then I ask: "How long does it take you to commute to work?" Everyone shares an estimate. "Does it always take that long?" No. "What changes?" Road conditions, weather, accidents, construction, car trouble.

This is a Complex problem. The underlying conditions are always shifting, so cause and effect can only be understood in hindsight. Product development works the same way - requirements change, technology evolves, and what the customer wants today may not be what they want next month.

For Complex problems, you need a framework built for change. Scrum is exactly that. It keeps work transparent, inspects results frequently, and adapts based on what the team learns. You cannot plan your way to a solution - you have to probe, sense what happens, and respond.

### Chaotic

Imagine driving in a country where nobody follows traffic laws. Cars run red lights, drive on whichever side of the road they feel like, and pedestrians walk wherever they want. That is Chaos - there is no relationship between cause and effect that you can discover in time to be useful.

In Chaos, you act first to stabilize the situation, then sense what is happening, then respond. The priority is to move out of Chaos and into one of the other domains as quickly as possible.

### Why This Matters

Most organizations are tackling Complex problems but using approaches designed for the Complicated domain (detailed upfront plans, Gantt charts, fixed scope). Cynefin helps explain why those approaches keep failing and why frameworks like Scrum - built around short feedback loops and adaptation - are a better fit.

For a deeper explanation, see: [Complexity](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/complexity)

### Assignment

Share your learnings from the Cynefin model in about 100 words in your personal Mural board. In particular, consider: which domain does most of the work in your organization fall into, and does the approach your organization uses match that domain?

2	title: "6.1 Product Vision"
3	status: published
4	slug: "a-csm/section-6-service-to-the-product-owner/6.1-product-vision"
5	sidebar:
6	  order: 701
7	tableOfContents: false
8	---
9	
10	The **Product Vision** is a shared understanding of the overall goal and purpose for creating a product. Your vision describes the motivation behind creating the product, it is not the product itself.
11	
12	The Product Vision provides purpose and direction for the team. Without a vision, a group of people have little reason to move beyond individual work silos and become a true collaborative team. In addition, without a vision the team will flounder their way through the product delivery process making best guesses instead of informed choices.
13	
14	For this reason, one of the first things I ask all new teams that I meet is, "Please tell me what your Product Vision is." To ensure that it's really the team's own understanding, I ask the Product Owner to leave the room first. Most teams can't answer the question because they don't understand the vision.
15	
16	### Product Vision is Shared Understanding
17	
18	In too many cases, Product Vision is decided by a central group and then handed out to the team. You can't magically take something created by one group and expect other people to understand it. The least effective model I have seen is when the Product Owner shares a PowerPoint of the vision with the victims. They will learn little and retain less. It is far more effective to invite the people who are building the product to be in the room and participating in co-creating the vision.tiation]
19	
20	### Vision Tools
21	If you ask most team members what they expect from a vision, they will suggest that it is a short, meaningless statement, written with nice sounding words. This type of vision has only limited value.
22	
23	There are a number of effective tools and exercises, but please remember that much of their value comes from the fact that the vision is co-created. The people who will build the product were present in the room when the vision was defined and so they understand why it is valuable and what it represents. If they're not present, then all of the tools below become fancy versions of a PowerPoint presentation containing a short, meaningless statement.
24	
25	- [Product Box](https://reqtest.com/en/knowledgebase/how-to-build-a-product-vision-box-and-clarify-your-software-goals/) – You create a physical box that would market the product in the real world. In the virtual world, you give people a fixed surface area in a virtual space like Mural - this is exactly what we do in oct Owner workshop. _This is a powerful tool because we're challenged to draw and, since we don't that very often, it sparks creativity (laughter, too)._
26	- [Vision Board](https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/the-product-vision-board/) – A one-page board that gets you to answer the following key questions/prompts: State your overarching goal; Who will benefit from the product; Needs or Pains these people have; … - We also practice with this tool in the CSPO workshop.
27	- [Pixar Pitch](https://prettyagile.com/2014/06/pitching-pixar-pitch/) – _Trigger warning: this will ruin all Pixar movies for you_ - Storytelling is one of the most effective ways to communicating an idea. A former Pixar editor (Emma Coates) noticed that Pixar movies follow a similar pattern: Once Upon a Time There Was \_\_\_. Every Day, \_\_\_. One Day\_\_\_. Because of That,\_\_\_. Because of That, \_\_\_. Until Finally \_\_\_.
28	- [Remember the future](https://spin.atomicobject.com/2017/11/30/design-thinking-remember-future/) – Imagine that it is 5 years in the future and your company has just released a milestone version of the product. Then imagine several months later, when your customers are overjoyed. Why are they delighted? The customers have been talking so much, there is a headline in the New York Times/Globe And Mail. What does it say? The exercise works because it is easier for our brains to look back on something, than it is to look forward.
29	
30	### Worked Example: Family Expense Tracker
31	
32	To see how a vision comes together, here is an example we will carry through the next several assignments.
33	
34	Most families have no clear picture of where their money actually goes. Receipts pile up, credit card statements go unreviewed, and cash purchases vanish without a trace.
35	
36	This app helps families track, reconcile, and understand their spending so they can align it with what they actually value. If you say you value travel but most of your monthly spending goes to meals out, the app makes that gap visible so you can make a conscious choice: change your spending or update your values.
37	
38	**How it works:**
39	- Scan, upload, or email receipts to the app
40	- Upload credit card and bank statements
41	- The app reconciles receipts against statements, categorizes expenses, and lets you track spending against your stated values
42	
43	**The core problem it solves:** Families currently spend hours on manual tracking and still miss cash and small purchases. This app saves time by automating reconciliation and makes previously untrackable items trackable.
44	
45	### Assignment
46	
47	Use any of the above tools to create a vision for a product you are working on. (Ideally, it would be co-created with your team.) Share a version when you are ready in your personal Mural board.
48

There are a number of effective tools and exercises, but please remember that much of their value comes from the fact that the vision is co-created. The people who will build the product were present in the room when the vision was defined and so they understand why it is valuable and what it represents. If they're not present, then all of the tools below become fancy versions of a PowerPoint presentation containing a short, meaningless statement.

- [Product Box](https://reqtest.com/en/knowledgebase/how-to-build-a-product-vision-box-and-clarify-your-software-goals/) – You create a physical box that would market the product in the real world. In the virtual world, you give people a fixed surface area in a virtual space like Mural - this is exactly what we do in oct Owner workshop. _This is a powerful tool because we're challenged to draw and, since we don't that very often, it sparks creativity (laughter, too)._
- [Vision Board](https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/the-product-vision-board/) – A one-page board that gets you to answer the following key questions/prompts: State your overarching goal; Who will benefit from the product; Needs or Pains these people have; … - We also practice with this tool in the CSPO workshop.
- [Pixar Pitch](https://prettyagile.com/2014/06/pitching-pixar-pitch/) – _Trigger warning: this will ruin all Pixar movies for you_ - Storytelling is one of the most effective ways to communicating an idea. A former Pixar editor (Emma Coates) noticed that Pixar movies follow a similar pattern: Once Upon a Time There Was \_\_\_. Every Day, \_\_\_. One Day\_\_\_. Because of That,\_\_\_. Because of That, \_\_\_. Until Finally \_\_\_.
- [Remember the future](https://spin.atomicobject.com/2017/11/30/design-thinking-remember-future/) – Imagine that it is 5 years in the future and your company has just released a milestone version of the product. Then imagine several months later, when your customers are overjoyed. Why are they delighted? The customers have been talking so much, there is a headline in the New York Times/Globe And Mail. What does it say? The exercise works because it is easier for our brains to look back on something, than it is to look forward.

### Worked Example: Family Expense Tracker

To see how a vision comes together, here is an example we will carry through the next several assignments.

Most families have no clear picture of where their money actually goes. Receipts pile up, credit card statements go unreviewed, and cash purchases vanish without a trace.

This app helps families track, reconcile, and understand their spending so they can align it with what they actually value. If you say you value travel but most of your monthly spending goes to meals out, the app makes that gap visible so you can make a conscious choice: change your spending or update your values.

**How it works:**
- Scan, upload, or email receipts to the app
- Upload credit card and bank statements
- The app reconciles receipts against statements, categorizes expenses, and lets you track spending against your stated values

**The core problem it solves:** Families currently spend hours on manual tracking and still miss cash and small purchases. This app saves time by automating reconciliation and makes previously untrackable items trackable.

### Assignment

Use any of the above tools to create a vision for a product you are working on. (Ideally, it would be co-created with your team.) Share a version when you are ready in your personal Mural board.

The coaching stance is the place we start from, the place we return, and ideally the place we include when using any of the other competencies. Watch-words of the coaching stance are maintaining neutrality, serving the client’s agenda, reducing client dependence, not colluding, and signature presence.
26	
27	### **Maintaining neutrality**
28	
29	 By neutrality, we mean the ability to “not vote” on your favorite position, for instance when the team is discussing a problem, or an individual is working something through for themselves, with your help. Neutrality is clear when using the Facilitating or Coaching competencies, but we extend it to Teaching and Mentoring. The neutrality we mean extends even to the point of assisting the client in choosing not to use Agile, if that is ‘what is trying to happen’ in their organization or is what the client chooses after full exploration of the consequences.
30	
31	### **Serving the client’s agenda**
32	
33	‘Client’ in this context could mean an individual, a team, an organizational department, or the whole organization. Each of these has an agenda. “Serving” could mean holding (balancing, reflecting, supporting) all of these agenda at the same time. The underlying belief: They are the experts in their own lives and organizations - they are whole and can make their own choices.
34	
35	### Not colluding
36	
37	The coach does not collude with the client’s desire to accommodate their dysfunctions or limitations. If the client reformulates their chosen Agile method to sidestep problems Agile has exposed, then the coach calls this out, reflecting the current situation, making plain what is actually happening, but without attachment or judgment. The coach does not “go along” with the compromise but, instead, recognizes the current situation for what it is, meets the client where they are, holds out the vision of Agile done well and continues to coach from a place of letting the coaching be loving, compassionate and uncompromising (Coaching Agile Teams, p. 81). While this may seem paradoxical, this approach is not inconsistent with Neutrality. On the one hand, we do not “pretend” with the client that they are really taking an Agile approach even when they are not. On the other hand, we do not resort to shaming or coercing them into doing it “the right way.” 
38	
39	### **Signature Presence**
40	
41	The concept of signature presence is from Mary Beth O’Neill in her book Executive Coaching with Backbone and Heart. We use it here to mean the Agile Coach must find their unique voice, their individual way of expressing their coaching, of taking a stand when necessary, and of being authentic while filling their role. This coaching stance is, for us, the default position as an Agile Coach. This stance makes what we do powerful, filled with integrity, and respectful of the client’s right to choose. Ideally applied in all eight competency areas, it is ultimately a distillation of, and largely borrowed from, the Coaching competency area and the world of professional coaching.
42

44	
45	Everything an Agile Coach does is for the sake of transferring a practice, skill, mindset or value to the client, striving to create a healthy agile ecosystem that is self- monitoring, self-correcting and self- sustaining. For instance, external Agile Coaches should build an organization’s ability to develop and sustain their own Coaches, developing them in the full breadth of the competencies described here. Internal Agile Coaches should build the capabilities of every Agilist and every team, trusting that there will always be more and better challenges to face.Source: [Developing Agile Coaches by Lyssa Adkins and Michael Spayd](https://www.agil8.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Agile-Coaching-Competencies-whitepaper-part-one.pdf)

We regularly need to explain Scrum and its benefits to people outside the team - managers, executives, and other stakeholders who may be skeptical or unfamiliar. A clear, concise framing makes all the difference. Focus on benefits and not Scrum itself.

### Framing Scrum for Stakeholders

Peter Stevens offers a useful way to describe Scrum in business terms:

> Scrum is a simple, team-based framework for solving complex problems, like creating great products or taking an organization to the next level. The essence of Scrum can be applied at any level of your organization:
>
> - **Cadence** - Inspect and adapt at frequent, regular intervals.
> - **Ownership** - Solve the whole problem in a small team, from idea to done.
> - **Speed** - Help the team and the organization improve and collaborate to deliver value faster.
> - **Tangible results** - Produce in cadence something you can use, sell, or test in real life.
> - **Alignment** - Speak to one specific person for decisions about the product.
> - **Leadership** - Lead by providing guidance and support, and know when to stay out of the way.
>
> "The purpose of an agile transformation is to restructure the company to optimize for speed and value generation."
>

Notice that this framing avoids Scrum jargon (no mention of Sprints, Product Backlogs, or ceremonies). It speaks in terms stakeholders care about: speed, value, ownership, and results. When you pitch Scrum to a stakeholder, lead with their problems and show how Scrum addresses them.

### Building Your Pitch
Imagine you encounter a business stakeholder who could benefit from Scrum but is not yet convinced. You have 1-3 minutes. How do you make the case?

A few tips:
- **Start with their pain.** What problem are they struggling with? Slow delivery? Misaligned priorities? Lack of visibility into progress?
- **Connect Scrum to their problem.** Use the framing above - pick the two or three points most relevant to their situation.
- **Keep it concrete.** Instead of "we inspect and adapt," try "every two weeks the team delivers working software and gets feedback, so we catch problems early instead of six months in."
- **Avoid jargon.** If you say "Sprint Retrospective" to someone who has never heard of Scrum, you have already lost them.

### Assignment

1. Think of a real stakeholder in your organization who could benefit from Scrum or who is not yet convinced. What are their biggest concerns or pain points?
2. Write a 1-3 minute pitch tailored to that stakeholder. Focus on the benefits that matter most to them, using language they would use. Share your pitch in your personal Mural board.

### Coaching Stances

What we call the “coaching stance” is for us the heart of the competency framework because it informs all the other competencies. The coaching stance is the place we start from, the place we return, and ideally the place we include when using any of the other competencies. Without the coaching stance, the work of an Agile Coach may become manipulative, ideological, and driven by the coach’s own desires—even when those desires are seemingly benign and believed to be in the ‘best interest’ of the client. Watch-words of the coaching stance are maintaining neutrality, serving the client’s agenda, reducing client dependence, not colluding, and signature presence.

### **Maintaining neutrality**

 By neutrality, we mean the ability to “not vote” on your favorite position, for instance when the team is discussing a problem, or an individual is working something through for themselves, with your help. Neutrality is clear when using the Facilitating or Coaching competencies, but we extend it to Teaching and Mentoring. The neutrality we mean extends even to the point of assisting the client in choosing not to use Agile, if that is ‘what is trying to happen’ in their organization or is what the client chooses after full exploration of the consequences.

### **Serving the client’s agenda**

‘Client’ in this context could mean an individual, a team, an organizational department, or the whole organization. Each of these has an agenda. “Serving” could mean holding (balancing, reflecting, supporting) all of these agenda at the same time. The underlying belief: They are the experts in their own lives and organizations - they are whole and can make their own choices.

### Not colluding

The coach does not collude with the client’s desire to accommodate their dysfunctions or limitations. If the client reformulates their chosen Agile method to sidestep problems Agile has exposed, then the coach calls this out, reflecting the current situation, making plain what is actually happening, but without attachment or judgment. The coach does not “go along” with the compromise but, instead, recognizes the current situation for what it is, meets the client where they are, holds out the vision of Agile done well and continues to coach from a place of letting the coaching be loving, compassionate and uncompromising (Coaching Agile Teams, p. 81). While this may seem paradoxical, this approach is not inconsistent with Neutrality. On the one hand, we do not “pretend” with the client that they are really taking an Agile approach even when they are not. On the other hand, we do not resort to shaming or coercing them into doing it “the right way.” 

### **Signature Presence**

The concept of signature presence is from Mary Beth O’Neill in her book Executive Coaching with Backbone and Heart. We use it here to mean the Agile Coach must find their unique voice, their individual way of expressing their coaching, of taking a stand when necessary, and of being authentic while filling their role. This coaching stance is, for us, the default position as an Agile Coach. This stance makes what we do powerful, filled with integrity, and respectful of the client’s right to choose. Ideally applied in all eight competency areas, it is ultimately a distillation of, and largely borrowed from, the Coaching competency area and the world of professional coaching.

### **Reducing client dependence**

Everything an Agile Coach does is for the sake of transferring a practice, skill, mindset or value to the client, striving to create a healthy agile ecosystem that is self- monitoring, self-correcting and self- sustaining. For instance, external Agile Coaches should build an organization’s ability to develop and sustain their own Coaches, developing them in the full breadth of the competencies described here. Internal Agile Coaches should build the capabilities of every Agilist and every team, trusting that there will always be more and better challenges to face.Source: [Developing Agile Coaches by Lyssa Adkins and Michael Spayd](https://www.agil8.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Agile-Coaching-Competencies-whitepaper-part-one.pdf)
